Objective Scoring vs Projective Interpretation

With the understanding that scores are a combination of a subject’s writing patterns and psychoanalytic interpretations, let’s split them into two categories.

Objective Scoring:

  • Word and Sentence Counts: Includes average word and sentence length, sentence fragments, and sentence variety.
  • Formatting and Structure: Evaluates line length, paragraph length, punctuation usage, and word frequency.
  • Readability: Quantifiable metrics determining how easily the text can be understood using various indices.

Projective Interpretation: 

  • Psychological Analysis: Psychoanalysts use their understanding of the human psyche and assign meanings to the patterns in an essay. 
  • Subjective Metrics: These scores are determined based on the richness of the content, which is how well a subject incorporates feelings and emotions, as well as how readable the essay is. 

The Psychological Basis of Projective Testing

Projective testing measures personality through open-ended prompts. One of the most cited theories is Rorschach’s, who suggested that responses to undefined tasks—like drawing a picture—reveal deeper thoughts, working out deeply formed defense mechanisms.

The Processing Speed Factor

Projective tests typically use time-limited tasks, such as writing essays under pressure, developing spontaneous responses to specific prompts. These are closely related to processing speed, which affects how quickly ideas can be generated. The same holds true for processing speed in IELTS exams. Tests evaluate how quickly thought processes occur, such as cognitive flexibility, which may also indicate processing speed exercises.

Implications for Test Design

  • Research is needed to comprehensively correlate the scores of projective test essays and the language tests.
  • If a similarity is found, additional tests may be developed to assess processing speed.
  • This will improve the accuracy of the current scoring mechanisms, resulting in better IELTS test results.

The Future of Projective Testing in IELTS

  1. Research: There is a need for more comprehensive studies that link projective essay scores to processing speed indicators.
  2. Development process measures like Timed Essay Writing Tests (TEWT) that focus on speed and complexity and precision of language 
  3. Test analysis: Continuous test result analysis over a longer time with a greater sample pool can give a complete picture of the identification of the fast processing speeds and the pattern of essay-writing

5. Inspiring Hope

A journal helps children to set and monitor their lifelong goals. Writing them down is proven to improve a child’s chances of achieving them.

Learn to use journaling prompts to keep a child on track. Ask questions like: “What are things you would like to know about in the future?” “What vaccine will be next?” or “What would it be like to visit Europa?” Using questions like this allows children to direct their thinking and learning towards a specific topic.

A fun way to do this is by having them write their own newspaper. Help them by asking questions like, “What would be the front-page news?” “Who would be the cast?” and “Where would these stories be published.”

This type of creative activity aids children in discovering new topics and their paths. All they need is a bank of words related to that topic as inspiration.

I ran through the scene over and over, terrified of what my classmates would say to me if I made a mistake. 

I always put so much pressure on myself to be perfect.

But when I stepped off stage in my real role and realized I didn't sound like myself, I felt awful. I'd built this vibrant character based on one-line memories from years ago.

As I had shared my memories, strangers had told me how sad my story was. They seemed fascinated by the fact that I, a young, healthy girl, had learned biomagnetism when dealing with an invisible illness. 

Even though I had been my authentic self, it felt like people were only interested in the dense pain that had defined my experiences with illness—which didn't match my view at the time, nor how I saw myself now. 

I'll never forget a group of classmates at rehearsal asked me what psychological factors made me depressed. It was just a curiosity of theirs. 

But when one of them asked if I had attempted suicide, another interrupted her: "Uh-oh, Zary, did you really just ask her that?" 

I hadn't met any other mentally ill people, nor had I paid attention to what it actually was. But it seemed accepted that people could ask whatever questions they wanted—a quietly recognized privilege of mental health. 

I didn't know how to explain my reaction to a question like that. And I was still around people who thought I was weak for having mental illness. So I felt ashamed for saying how that question made me feel out of the ordinary.

I couldn't help feeling uncomfortable in that environment anymore. I wondered if I even belonged in it. 

Only then did I feel safe if I went to school early and ate lunch alone. It was the only time I felt trusted enough to express myself as I was.

I needed to be authentic again.

Practicing taking upsetting situations and reframing them means you double-check your thoughts and the facts in front of you to determine if you do in fact need to dwell on it... or not. Interpreting your fear

After recounting your fears, assess if these are temporary or will likely linger throughout your life. In most cases, it’s normal for nerves or doubts to occur during significant events like job interviews, presentations, or public speaking. This happens to many people, making it an ordinary anxiety. However, you could experience persistent negative thoughts about yourself, like “I’m not good enough” that have been happening for a long time, even if your circumstances change. Negative self-presence may give way to more severe anxiety (i.e., phobias and post-traumatic stress disorder), depression, and personality disorders. Identifying whether they stay with you or lessen is critical to helping your mental well-being.

When persistent negative self-perception appears

For ongoing challenging situations, making a change could be beneficial. Whether it’s how you perceive yourself based on these prevalent negative thoughts or switching from a job you don’t love to one you do—or seeking professional guidance from therapists or career coaches—to help you gain new insights and release you from self-perception constraints.

Reflect, inquire, and act

Negative thoughts, while distressing, can be reframed through self-reflection and action — you must be willing to challenge the parts of yourself to think positively about yourself. Start by examining the thoughts—”Am I generalising? Is there evidence against this?” Then, challenge your story by trying to replace it with a more positive one and changing what’s within your control. Once you start, don’t be discouraged. It is natural to have setbacks, but you must be persistent to stay on track if change is needed.

Facing your fears

If you want to expand your comfort zone and be less restricted by what you first thought (how you initially viewed yourself), the most important step is simply being courageous – forging forward, ignoring some of your self-doubts, and proving that you are far and more competent than what you have limited yourself to all this time.

Adopt a Growth Mindset

Sid Mead

Morning came too quickly for poor Nina. She got up and rushed to prepare for the day, trying to put her best face forward, until she recalled that she had told her parents that she had won the competition. She was not sure what to do now. The whole way to school, the same question kept running through her mind.
"Do I tell mum and da what really happened?"
She did not know the answer. Knowing the implications of not doing so, she fidgeted. Days came and went. Autumn slipped into winter. One day, in the beginning of May, she plucked up the courage to have a proper talk with her parents. Mr. and Mrs. Nielsen ushered Nina into the kitchen and asked her to help prepare lunch. The smell of bread baking filled the kitchen with golden roux dripping the apetitales. As Nina stood at the door, her parents asked her if there was something on her mind."Yes, please sit down," she said, her voice trembling a little bit, "Dad, Mum, this is it. I lied about winning the Roman Day time travel competition. It was all a hoax. The time machine was a made up replica, like a costume in Disneyland. The prizes too, were mostly those fancy political achievements, you know the Nobel Prize and the like. I'm so sorry, I was afraid to disappoint you and I am telling the truth now. Please do not disown me..."
Who would expect to hear something like that?
Luckily for Nina, her parents said,"Come on dear, what are you thinking? We would never disown our lovely child! Let's enjoy some nice bread rolls and hot butter instead, shall we?"
Nina felt a huge burden lifted from her shoulders and she could finally be herself, for really, when had she stopped being herself.
Evie de Bruijne

If you take something in, you consume or absorb it. The most common things we "swallow" are food, criticism, pain, etc.
